lessons.0.slides.1.title: The Role of the Sommelier
lessons.0.slides.1.content: A professional sommelier is far more than a beverage-service person: they are the designer of the dining experience, the guest's personal wine consultant, and the bridge between the restaurant and the domaine. In a Michelin-starred restaurant the sommelier must possess deep wine knowledge, refined taste, elegant service skills, and the ability to collaborate closely with the kitchen.

lessons.0.slides.3.title: The Art and Science of Decanting
lessons.0.slides.3.content: Decanting serves three purposes: separating sediment, promoting oxidation, and releasing aromas. Young Burgundy reds (within 10 years) typically benefit from 1–2 hours in a decanter; older vintages (20+ years) need only brief decanting or simple bottle breathing. White wines usually do not need decanting, but top white Burgundies (Meursault, Puligny-Montrachet) can benefit from a short decant (15–30 minutes).
lessons.0.slides.4.title: ⏱️ Burgundy Red Decanting Time Guide (Adjusted by Age)
lessons.0.slides.4.content: Young reds need long decanting (1–2 hours); older vintages need only 15–30 minutes. Over-decanting loses aromatics — timing is everything!

lessons.1.slides.1.title: The Fundamental Principles of Food Pairing
lessons.1.slides.1.content: Food pairing with Burgundy emphasises 'balance' and 'enhancement': the wine should not overwhelm the food, nor should the food mask the wine's subtlety. Pinot Noir's high acidity, delicate tannins, and elegant style make it especially suited to refined French cuisine, game, mushrooms, and poultry. Chardonnay's creamy texture and minerality pair perfectly with seafood, shellfish, poultry, and cream sauces.

lessons.2.slides.1.title: The Tiered Design of a Burgundy Wine List
lessons.2.slides.1.content: A great Burgundy wine list must span different price points, regions, and styles so that guests of every budget can find the right choice. Recommended structure: entry-level (Régionale, Village) 30–40%, mid-range (Premier Cru, notable villages) 40–50%, premium (Grand Cru, prestigious producers) 10–20%, special vintages and rare wines 5–10%.

lessons.4.slides.1.title: The Environmental Conditions of a Professional Cellar
lessons.4.slides.1.content: Ideal cellar conditions: temperature 12–14°C (constant), humidity 60–70%, no light (especially UV), no vibration, good ventilation. Burgundy wines are particularly sensitive to temperature fluctuations — a swing of more than 5°C accelerates ageing. Humidity too low causes corks to dry and shrink; too high promotes mould growth.
lessons.4.slides.2.title: 🌡️ Professional Cellar Environmental Parameters (Ideal vs Danger Zones)
lessons.4.slides.2.content: Temperature 12–14°C, humidity 60–70% is the ideal range. Above 18°C or below 50% humidity will damage wine quality. Constant temperature and humidity are the keys!

lessons.6.slides.1.title: Reading the Guest's Needs
lessons.6.slides.1.content: A professional sommelier must quickly gauge the guest's knowledge level, budget, and taste preferences. Avoid over-technical language that intimidates beginners, but never underestimate the knowledge of a seasoned wine lover. Use open questions ('What style do you prefer?') rather than closed ones ('Red or white?') to guide the conversation.
lessons.6.slides.2.title: 💬 The Golden Rules of Communication
lessons.6.slides.2.points.0: Listen first — understand the guest's real needs
lessons.6.slides.2.points.1: Offer options — give 2–3 suggestions rather than a single recommendation
lessons.6.slides.2.points.2: Tell stories — move people with stories, not data
lessons.6.slides.2.points.3: Respect the budget — never make the guest feel pressured
lessons.6.slides.2.points.4: Educative selling — provide value, not just a pitch
lessons.6.slides.2.points.5: Build relationships — long-term guests are the core asset
